extracted.intended_audience: readers and students of military history; military professionals interested in colonial/frontier campaign practices
extracted.subtask_description: Narrative-derived principles and practical standards for conducting and evaluating British colonial/frontier military operations (logistics, cavalry employment, village-punishment, casualty evacuation, assault formations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Transport and mobility (logistics)
rubrics_metrics.description: "Transport—the life and soul of an army—is an even more vital factor here than in less undeveloped countries. The mobility of a brigade depends entirely on its pack animals."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Loss of pack animals (mules) or high numbers of wounded can render a brigade immobile; restoring mobility requires evacuating the wounded to base and reconstituting units. Examples: many mules killed on the 14th; Sir Bindon Blood sought to 'restore its mobility by getting the wounded sent down to the base.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Force reconstitution and unit replacement
rubrics_metrics.description: When units are decimated by disease or combat, they must be exchanged or replaced to maintain fighting effectiveness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical steps include rotating/regiment swaps (e.g., 11th Bengal Lancers succeeded by Guides Cavalry; Buffs exchanged for Royal West Kent) and reassigning batteries and battalions to rebuild striking power after losses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legitimacy and rationale for punitive village-burning
rubrics_metrics.description: The author argues that when villagers attack and then retire to inaccessible hills, the only practical remedy is destroying their property: 'Their villages are made hostages for their good behavior.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Justification rests on inability to catch/punish attackers in hills, impracticality of discriminating 'guilty' houses, and the view that houses on the frontier function as fortifications. The author contrasts this with other theatres (Cuba) and criticizes euphemistic official language ('visited and punished', 'fortifications were demolished').

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition of villages as fortifications (operational fact)
rubrics_metrics.description: "All along the Afghan border every man's house is his castle. The villages are the fortifications, the fortifications are the villages. Every house is loopholed..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because dwellings are fortified and used for combat, military operations cannot treat houses as separate civilian property; tactical decisions (including destruction) must account for the defensive use of habitation structures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of cavalry for reconnaissance
rubrics_metrics.description: "Major Beatson made daily expeditions... This use of cavalry is an entirely new one on the frontier — it having been thought that it was dangerous to employ them in this way."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cavalry can collect critical intelligence even over broken ground if used boldly; reconnaissance expeditions toward valleys and passes supply information needed for operations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cavalry employment for flank protection and skirmishing
rubrics_metrics.description: In mountain actions cavalry are often tasked to protect a flank, using carbines rather than traditional charge formations: 'The task ... is to protect one of the flanks. ... it is necessary for the men to use their carbines.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tactics include dismounted small groups returning fire, mounted patrols concealed in nullahs/hollows to chase off attackers, and extending lines to cover approaches. Example: two weak squadrons held a valley in check for five hours, preventing enemy flanking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mounting/retirement under fire (practical drill)
rubrics_metrics.description: When retiring under fire, troops should mount in a covered, staged sequence with other troops providing covering fire: described sequence of first troop mounting while second covers retirement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Order mounting so one troop covers the other; use parting volleys, then mount and extend into an extended line; expect immediate fire during mounting — coordination and timed covering fire reduce casualties (example narration of a squadron mounting and retiring with minimal hits).

rubrics_metrics.name: Infantry-artillery formation and coordination in mountain assaults
rubrics_metrics.description: Brigade attack formation and the combined use of infantry and mountain/field artillery determine success on broken terrain (example Agrah attack: cavalry left, Guides and Royal West Kent centre, 31st Punjaub on right, 38th Dogras reserve).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mountain batteries throw shells over infantry to clear higher slopes; inadequate troop numbers and gaps between units permit flanking by enemy, causing most losses. Concentration of artillery (more and heavier guns) was planned to break strongholds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Casualty evacuation and field surgery logistics
rubrics_metrics.description: Provision of transport for wounded (camels, doolies, stretchers), prepared operating tables and surgeons is essential; conveyances can be exhausted and wounded must sometimes be carried by comrades.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arrange camels/doolies early, have surgeons and improvised operating tables ready (medical boxes, waterproof sheets). Expect overflow of casualties; practical methods (tying bodies to mules, carrying wounded by comrades) may be necessary in rough country.

rubrics_metrics.name: Training value of frequent skirmishes and small actions
rubrics_metrics.description: "Such affairs as these were of almost daily occurrence during the time that the 2nd Brigade occupied the camp at Inayat Kila. They were of the greatest value in training the soldiers."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regular small-scale engagements (foraging skirmishes, patrol actions) develop soldiers' skills, confidence, and steadiness under fire; they serve both tactical and training purposes.
